playbook:
My playbook for next time:

When a lot is put up, I first check my value for it against the standing bid. If value minus standing bid is small (say under 10), I pass — thin margins invite being topped into overpaying anyway.

In round 1, I open at or just above the minimum raise. There's no reason to bid big early: the opener only sets a floor, and my real decision comes in round 2. This episode that kept my round-1 exposure tiny (4, 8, 4, 4) and I lost nothing by it — opponents' round-1 bids revealed how much they wanted the lot before I had to commit.

In round 2, if the standing bid is still well below my value, I bid decisively — one large step, roughly two-thirds of my value or high enough that any counter must exceed my value. This worked: opponents who wanted the lot more than I did had to pay above my value to beat me (they paid 42 against my value 36, 40 against my 50), and when they couldn't, I won at a price well under my value (33 against 44, 20 against 27).

If the standing bid in round 2 is at or above my value, I pass without hesitation. Lot 5, standing bid 20 against my value 11 — passing there was clearly right, and I should keep doing it instantly, not deliberate.

My round-2 big jump is a ceiling-setting move, not a guaranteed winner. Twice opponents simply bid past it and paid more than my value — that is the system working, not failing. I should not feel the urge to chase after my jump is topped; once the standing bid exceeds roughly my two-thirds point, I let it go.

If my value is below the estimate, I should be much more reluctant to bid than I was. Lot 4 (value 27, estimate 39) I won at 20 for a thin +7, but only because round 2 closed low. If the round-1 standing bid from an opponent is already above, say, half my value on a below-estimate lot, I pass in round 2 rather than jump — the +7 I got there isn't worth the times I'd win at 25-27 for near-zero or get pushed past value.

I keep a strict running budget ledger. My stated budgets were again inconsistent (26, then 76, then 92, 67...). Before every reply I recompute: budget = starting budget minus the prices I actually paid for lots won, minus any live bid standing this round. I state that number and nothing else. A sloppy ledger risks bids I can't back or money I strand.

Money unspent at the end is worth nothing, so on the last lot, if the price is below my value, I bid up to nearly my full remaining budget rather than hold back. I didn't get to test this (final lot price exceeded my value), but the logic stands.

Overall pattern to repeat: minimal round-1, one decisive round-2 jump bounded by my value, hard pass when price reaches value. That produced +18 with no overpayments.

# Playbook for ref_auction

**Core rule: never bid above my value minus expected extra raises.** When the standing bid is high relative to my value, passing costs nothing. Only bid when standing_bid + raise(s) stays comfortably below my private value.

**When shown a lot, I first compute margin = my value − standing high bid.**
- If margin < ~2 minimum raises, I pass immediately.
- If margin is large in round 1, I bid only the minimum raise. Small raises keep my final price low even if I get outbid — being outbid cheaply is fine.
- I never jump-bid above the minimum in round 1; that only burns money when I win.

**Round 2 is a sealed final offer — bid for the whole margin, not just one tick.** This episode proved it: on a lot worth 44 I bid only 12 in round 2 and lost to 33, leaving ~31 of surplus on the table. In round 2 there is no further exposure — if I think a rival's final bid will land around X, and X < my value, I should bid near my best estimate of what it takes, not the minimum raise. A good default: bid up to roughly 60–75% of my value when margin is large, or to just under my value when competition has been fierce on this lot. Minimum raises in round 2 only win when nobody else wants the lot, which is exactly when I'd have won anyway.

**Budget tokens got scrambled — this is a hard rule now.** Before every reply I recompute budget as: current budget minus nothing (bids only cost money when they *win*). Lost lots cost nothing; won lots deduct their price. I stated [budget: 100] after starting at 30 — never again. State the correct running number, formatted exactly as `[budget: N]` on its own line, paired with `[bid: N]` or `[bid: pass]`. Never mash tokens onto one line.

**When a lot is worth less to me than its estimate, I only bid if the standing price is far below my value.** Competitors who value it more will outbid me anyway. Opening with a minimum bid on a low-value lot is a cheap option; I take it only when no one has bid yet, and I fold the moment I'm raised. This worked on lot 4: opened at 8, folded at 20 against value 27.

**Results so far are a price signal — use them.** Rivals paid 42, 33, 20 for comparable lots. If they've been paying near or above estimate, my round-2 sealed bid needs to be aggressive to win high-margin lots; if they've been cheap, minimum raises suffice.

**Across lots: preserve budget for high-margin lots.** A big-margin lot later is worth more than a thin-margin win now. I skip contests where my edge is under ~20% of my value unless the price is still trivially low.

**Never let a bid exceed my value.** Absolute cap on any bid = my value for that lot. Round 2 is the one place I can approach that cap deliberately, because there is no chance of being raised afterward.

PLAYBOOK — ref_auction

- The only bid that matters is round 2. Round 1 bids never win anything for me; they only show rivals my interest and set a floor I then have to outbid myself. So in round 1, when a lot already has a standing bid, I pass.
- In round 2, I bid once, decisively, at a level I'm willing to pay — not the minimum raise. If surplus is large, I jump to roughly half-way between the standing bid and my value; small increments just invite being outbid at the buzzer.
- Watch for a rival who goes quiet after round 1: when bidder 1 stopped pushing on lot 5, my decisive 20 against a 6 standing bid was uncontested and left big margin. Rivals' round-1 aggression varies by lot; use their round-1 bid size, not just the estimate, to judge how hard they'll fight in round 2.
- Before bidding in round 2, compute value minus bid. If surplus is thin (under ~20% of value), pass — rivals routinely push prices toward estimate, and winning thin lots is how you lose. Passing lot 4 (value 32, standing 20) was correct.
- Estimate is a weak anchor: lots 1 and 2 sold well above or at prices unrelated to my value signals. Bid off MY value and the standing bid only, not the estimate.
- Don't enter round 1 just because the standing bid is small. On lot 2 I planned to "strike in round 2," which worked: passing round 1 and jumping in round 2 is my standard pattern.
- A winning round-2 jump sometimes ends the auction at my own number (lot 1 won at 42 with no counter, lot 5 won at 20). Since there are only 2 rounds, my round-2 bid is final — bid as if rivals can't respond after it, because they can't. That means my jump only needs to beat the standing bid plus a plausible round-2 raise, not deter future bidding. Bid a bit lower than "halfway to value" when the standing bid is already substantial — the buzzer protects me.
- Budget accounting: my stated budget must decrease by exactly my winning-bid payments, no more. This episode I let the budget drift (8, 58, 100) with no consistent subtraction — that must not happen again. Track: budget shown last, minus winning-bid payments, minus nothing else. Passing rounds don't change it. Losing bids don't change it either.
- If a lot has NO standing bid in round 1 (bid is 0), a single minimum-raise opening bid is acceptable — it may stand, or be raised only modestly, and it costs almost nothing. But once anyone else has bid, I wait for round 2.
- Total score = sum of (value − price) over lots won. I ended +26 on one lot (55 − 42 = +13... verify arithmetic when scoring) plus a cheap lot-5 win — wait, lot 5 was won at 20 with value 33, and lot 2's bid of 21 apparently didn't win. Don't assume my round-2 jump wins; rivals can top it within round 2. Next time, when a lot matters a lot, bid closer to full value to close it out.
- Roughly one decisive win per few lots at good surplus is enough for a positive score; I don't need every lot, just the ones where I end round 2 with a clear margin.
